name: Swift Run
lithology: Fine to medium-grained sandstone deposited in a prodelta setting. Poorly-sorted subrounded to subangular grains range from <0.03 to 2 mm in diameter. Detrital fragments have diverse compositions, including olivine and pyroxene grains, possible alteration minerals rich in Si and Al (phyllosilicates), and lithic fragments. A fine-grained matrix or cement appears depleted in Si and Al and enriched in Fe and Mg, much of which is interpreted to be Fe-Mg carbonate. Evidence of hydration, Na and Cl salts, and oxidation (ferric Fe) were also detected.
summary: Swift Run and Skyland, the pair of cores representing the fifth sample target of the Mars 2020 mission, were collected from Skinner Ridge, an outcrop of the Lower Rockytop member of the Hawksbill Gap region of the western Jezero delta front. Skinner Ridge lies at the base of ~6.5 vertical meters of exposed sedimentary rock layers of Rockytop (Figures 1 - 4) and is likely to be in place. The outcrop is a horizontally layered, medium-grained clastic sedimentary rock and has a similar sandstone lithology as Betty’s Rock, a float block of the Upper Rockytop member; its upper surface has low relief (Figures 3, 5). We sampled this sedimentary rock because it is from a low stratigraphic position within the western Jezero delta and contains a heterogeneous population of detrital materials deposited into the delta when a lake was present. At least some of these materials most likely derived from outside Jezero crater in the Neretva Vallis watershed. The Swift Run and Skyland cores were collected from a stratigraphic position that is ~3 vertical meters above the Hazeltop and Bearwallow cores collected from the Hogwallow Flats member, only ~20 m to the southwest (Figures 2, 4).

name: Hazeltop
lithology: Fine-grained, well-sorted sedimentary rock likely deposited in a lacustrine setting; a sulfate- bearing coarse mudstone. The rock is rich in weakly-hydrated Mg-Fe sulfate. Also detected were small amounts of Fe-Mg-clay minerals, hydrated silica or Al-clay minerals, and possibly carbonates. Numerous fluorescence detections may arise from aromatic organic compounds. The rock is cut by scattered veins and patches enriched in Ca sulfate, likely anhydrite, whereas the sulfate in the rock matrix is more magnesian.
summary: Hazeltop and Bearwallow, the pair of cores representing the sixth sample target of the Mars 2020 mission, were collected from Wildcat Ridge, an outcrop of the Hogwallow Flats member of the Hawksbill Gap region of the western Jezero delta front. Wildcat Ridge lies near the base of ~3 vertical meters of exposed sedimentary rock layers of Hogwallow Flats (Figures 1 - 5) and is likely to be in place. The outcrop is a horizontally layered, fine-grained, and well-sorted sedimentary rock; it is a sulfate- bearing coarse mudstone (Figures 3, 5). We sampled this sedimentary rock because it is from a low stratigraphic position within the exposed delta and contains a fine-grained texture, likely deposited on the floor of a lake. The rock is rich in weakly-hydrated Mg-Fe sulfate with evidence of small amounts of Fe-Mg clay minerals, hydrated silica or Al-clay minerals, and possibly carbonates. Thus, this rock has high potential for biosignature preservation.
sample_type: Fine-grained, well-sorted sedimentary rock; a sulfate-bearing coarse mudstone.

name: Shuyak
lithology: Fine-grained, well-sorted sedimentary rock likely deposited in a lacustrine setting; an olivine- bearing coarse mudstone. The rock primarily contains detrital olivine and aqueous alteration products of olivine (e.g., serpentine) plus minor salts. Minor phases detected may include chromite, ilmenite, apatite, and zircon/baddeleyite. No clear evidence of sand-sized pyroxene or feldspar was observed. The rock contains little, if any, evidence of sulfate minerals and a possible/weak fluorescence signal potentially related to organics.
summary: Shuyak and Mageik, the pair of cores representing the seventh sample target of the Mars 2020 mission, were collected from Amalik, an outcrop of the Enchanted Lake member of the Cape Nukshak region of the western Jezero delta front. Amalik lies near the base of the exposed delta sedimentary rocks in the Cape Nukshak region, ~4 vertical meters below the rim of Cape Nukshak (i.e., the Alagnak outcrop) (Figures 1 - 5) and is likely to be in place. The outcrop is a horizontally layered, fine-grained, and well-sorted sedimentary rock; it is an olivine-bearing coarse mudstone (Figures 3, 5). We sampled this sedimentary rock because it is from a low stratigraphic position within the western Jezero delta and contains a fine-grained texture, likely deposited on to the floor of a lake. The rock primarily contains detrital olivine with evidence for hydration and aqueous alteration products (e.g., serpentine), phyllosilicates, dolomite and some silica. Thus, this rock has potential for biosignature preservation.
sample_type: Fine-grained, well-sorted sedimentary rock; an olivine-bearing coarse mudstone.

name: Kukaklek
lithology: Fine-grained, moderately sorted sedimentary rock likely deposited in a lacustrine setting; a sulfate-bearing fine sandstone. The rock is rich in weakly-hydrated Mg-Fe sulfate. Small amounts of Fe- Mg-clay minerals, possible carbonates, and hydrated silica or Al-clay minerals were also detected. The rock is cut by scattered veins and patches of Ca sulfate, likely anhydrite, whereas the sulfate in the rock matrix is more magnesian. Fluorescence signals are consistent with a mix of aromatic compounds, and are associated with the calcium sulfate patches.
summary: Kukaklek, the core representing the eighth sample target of the Mars 2020 mission, was collected from Hidden Harbor, an outcrop of the Yori Pass member of the Cape Nukshak region of the western Jezero delta front. Hidden Harbor lies above the exposed delta sedimentary rocks in the Cape Nukshak region, is ~15 vertical meters below the break in slope that defines the base of Whale Mountain (Figures 1 - 5) and is likely to be in place. The outcrop is a horizontally layered, fine-grained, and moderately sorted sedimentary rock; a sulfate-bearing fine sandstone (Figures 3, 5). We sampled this sedimentary rock because it is from a low stratigraphic position within the western Jezero delta and contains a fine- grained texture, likely deposited on to the floor of a lake. The rock contains abundant weakly hydrated Mg-Fe sulfate with evidence of small amounts of Fe-Mg-clay minerals, possible carbonates, hydrated silica or Al-clay minerals, and sulfate veins and patches likely of diagenetic origin. Thus, this rock has high potential for biosignature preservation.
sample_type: Fine-grained, moderately sorted sedimentary rock; a sulfate-bearing very fine sandstone.

name: Atmo Mountain
lithology: Regolith sample consists of a mixture of coarse grains up to ~ 5 mm diameter, finer sand of various grades, silt, and likely (not directly resolved) atmospheric dust. Primary (igneous) minerals include variably altered olivine, pyroxene, Fe- and Ti-oxides, and possibly quartz. Secondary phases include sulfates and carbonates and possibly Fe-Mg phyllosilicates. Phosphates and aluminosilicates may be primary or secondary or both.
summary: The Atmo Mountain and Crosswind Lake regolith samples were collected from the megaripple Observation Mountain (Figure 1, 2). Observation Mountain was selected for sampling because it is a large megaripple with sufficient size to allow sample acquisition and workspace analyses, and because it was thought to be less mobile than other potential sampling targets, allowing investigation of a surface likely impacted by martian surface processes such as crust formation. The rover’s wheel was used to scuff the megaripple to expose material beneath the surface; this subsurface material likely dominates the regolith samples. The wheel scuff wall (Fultons Falls) (Figure 2) provided an in situ exposure of subsurface material for observations by Mastcam-Z, Supercam, and, at moderate standoff, WATSON. The wheel scuff tailings pile provided a positive-relief accumulation of sub-surface material that was large enough to be approached closely by PIXL, SHERLOC, and WATSON (target Topographers Peak) to compare with Mastcam-Z multispectral observations and Supercam observations (Geographic Harbor). The floor of the wheel scuff cavity (the wheel track) also was analyzed with Supercam and Mastcam-Z (target Funnel Creek). These multiple observations of the subsurface material help place the returned material, which was unavoidably mixed during collection, into context.

name: Pelican Point
lithology: Moderately to poorly sorted medium to coarse grained rock, probably a sandstone deposited in a currently uncertain setting (possibilities include shoreline, fluviolacustrine, and aeolian). Less likely, an altered igneous deposit (intrusive, extrusive, or pyroclastic). Bulk composition is that of an altered basalt. Major primary minerals occurring as sand-sized grains are olivine, pyroxene, and altered silicates. Also present are Fe-Ti-Cr spinels, phyllosilicates, and small amounts of feldspar. Fe/Mg-carbonate (including hydrated carbonate) and minor Fe/Mg sulfate are present as rims, coatings, or cavity infilling. Silica fills interstitial space between grains and may be a cement.
summary: Pelican Point is the first sample of the Margin Campaign exploring rocks exposed between the western edge of the Jezero fan and the inner crater rim. It was collected at the Hans Amundsen Memorial Workspace 1 (previously Point Edgar) on sol 923 in the Mandu Wall region of the Margin unit (Figures 1- 2). The associated abrasion patch Amherst Point was acquired on sol 915. The Mandu Wall region consists of a local topographic low in the Margin unit where it intersects the fan-associated Blocky unit. The Margin unit appears to uncomformably underlie the Blocky and Curvilinear units of the fan (Figure 3), but its stratigraphic position relative to strata deeper in the fan (e.g., the Shenandoah formation) is unknown. The origin of the Margin unit is also uncertain, but sedimentary deposition in a shoreline, fluviolacustrine, or aeolian setting is considered most likely. In the absence of strong evidence for sedimentary structures, the Margin unit could alternatively be a pyroclastic or extrusive or intrusive igneous deposit.
sample_type: medium to coarse sandstone with alteration phases (or possibly an altered igneous rock)

name: Lefroy Bay
lithology: Moderately to poorly sorted medium to coarse grained rock, probably a sandstone, deposited in a currently uncertain setting (possibilities include shoreline, fluviolacustrine and aeolian). Less likely, an altered igneous deposit (intrusive, extrusive, or pyroclastic). Bulk composition is that of an altered basalt. Also present are Fe-Ti-Cr spinels, phyllosilicates, small amounts of feldspar and chlorine-bearing phases. Mg/Fe-carbonate and Mg-sulfate are present. summary: Lefroy Bay is the second sample of the Margin Campaign exploring rocks exposed between the western edge of the Jezero fan and the inner crater rim. It was cored at the Lake Newell outcrop on sol 942 in the Turquoise Bay region of the Margin (Figures 1-2). Lefroy Bay is associated with the Bills Bay abrasion patch, acquired on sol 935. Turquoise Bay represents a local topographic high of the Margin unit targeted for investigation because it contains a particularly strong CRISM carbonate signature. The Margin unit appears to uncomformably underlie the Blocky and Curvilinear units of the fan (Figure 3), but its stratigraphic position relative to strata deeper in the fan (e.g., the Shenandoah formation) is unknown. The origin of the Margin unit is also uncertain, but sedimentary deposition in a shoreline, fluviolacustrine, or aeolian setting is considered most likely. In the absence of strong evidence for sedimentary structures, the Margin unit could alternatively be a pyroclastic or extrusive or intrusive igneous deposit.
sample_type: medium to coarse sandstone with alteration phases (or possibly an altered igneous rock)

name: Comet Geyser
lithology: Moderately to poorly sorted coarse sandstone or a thoroughly aqueously altered mafic to ultramafic igneous rock deposited in an unknown setting (possibilities include shoreline, aeolian, fluviolacustrine, pyroclastic or intrusive igneous deposit). Mineralogy is dominated by Mg-Fe carbonates, silica, altered silicates, and phyllosilicates; also present are Fe-Ti-Cr spinel, Ca-sulfate, and possibly olivine, pyroxene, sepiolite, and a chlorine-bearing phase.
summary: Comet Geyser is the third sample of the Margin campaign exploring rocks exposed between the western edge of the Jezero fan and the inner crater rim. It was collected at Bunsen Peak in the western Margin on sol 1088 (Figures 1-2). The associated abrasion patch Castle Geyser was acquired on sol 1080. The western Margin lacks clear sedimentary structures at the outcrop level, including at Bunsen Peak. Here the landscape consists of resistant dark-toned high-standing and often massive outcrop interbedded with lighter-toned low-lying rocks. This appearance is distinctly different from the eastern Margin from which the Pelican Point and Lefroy Bay samples were collected, where mostly tabular or plate-like outcrop occurs in a relatively flat landscape. Although the elevation of Comet Geyser is 25 meters higher than Lefroy Bay, their relative position within any Margin stratigraphy has not been established. The Margin unit appears to lie unconformably below the Blocky unit of the fan (Figure 3), but its position relative to strata deeper in the fan (e.g., the Shenandoah formation) is unknown. The primary origin of the Margin unit is also uncertain. In the absence of readily interpreted sedimentary structures, if the Margin unit is sedimentary, it may have been deposited in almost any setting: shoreline, fluviolacustrine, aeolian or pyroclastic. Alternatively, Comet Geyser could be an intrusive mafic to ultramafic igneous rock, highly altered by interaction with fluids. In retrospect, the same origin could also apply to the two previous Margin samples.
sample_type: coarse sandstone or altered (carbonated, serpentinized) mafic to ultramafic igneous rock

name: Sapphire Canyon
lithology: Fine-grained silicate rock with abundant calcium sulfate veins. Likely a fluvial or lacustrine sedimentary rock. Tan-colored matrix is dominantly an Al-rich silicate, probably phyllosilicate with minor iron phosphate, calcium sulfate, iron sulfide and possibly Fe-Mg-sulfate. The silicate part of the rock has spatially distributed sub-mm-size nodules and mm-size reaction fronts that may be reduction spots. Light-toned veins consist of Ca-sulfate that contains mm-size olivine grains. Likely reduction spots and Raman G-band organics constitute potential biosignatures in this sample.
summary: Sapphire Canyon is the first and currently the only sample collected within the Bright Angel unit, a layered light-toned and pervasively-veined region of low-lying rock outcrop exposed on the floor of Neretva Vallis where the channel exits the walls of the Jezero rim and enters the crater (Figures 1-5). The core and its associated abrasion patch Apollo Temple were acquired at the Beaver Falls workspace between sols 1211 and 1215. Beaver Falls lies within a transitional region between the typical veined and light-toned Bright Angel rocks to the south and darker-toned rocks (e.g., Steamboat Mountain) that occur close to the likely contact with the Margin unit to the north. Bright Angel is topographically lower than observed outcrops of the Margin unit, but the temporal relationship between the two is uncertain. Bright Angel may be older and may have been buried beneath the Margin Unit, or it may be younger, having been deposited into a channel carved into the Margin unit. The depositional setting of Bright Angel is currently unknown, with favored hypotheses for its origin including subaqueous sedimentary (fluvial, lacustrine), and volcaniclastic. Bright Angel has experienced strong aqueous alteration.
sample_type: fine-grained sulfate-veined sedimentary rock with dominantly clay/silt-size grains
